ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the diagram, $ \triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADE$, and $\angle EAB = 120^\circ$, $\angle B = 30^\circ$, $\angle CAD = 10^\circ$, what is the degree measure of $\angle CFD$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Since $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADE$, \\
it follows that $\angle EAD = \angle CAB$, \\
and since $\angle EAB = 120^\circ$ and $\angle CAD = 10^\circ$, \\
it follows that $\angle EAD = \angle CAB = 55^\circ$, \\
therefore, $\angle CFD = \angle FAB + \angle B = 10^\circ + 55^\circ + 30^\circ = \boxed{95^\circ}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, A is at the lower left, B is at the lower right, and line segment AB is approximately horizontal; from A upward there is ray AD, D is above, and F is located on AD. E is at the upper left of A, and ray AE and ray AB form the larger angle ∠EAB. C is located at the upper right of A, and line segment AC is connected to A. In the figure there is also an oblique line from G at the upper left passing through F and C and extending to B at the lower right, therefore B, C, F are collinear; F is the intersection point of AD and this oblique line. Reasoning: As can be seen from the figure, ∠EAB is divided in order into ∠EAD, ∠DAC, ∠CAB, among which ∠DAC = ∠CAD = 10°. It is known that △ABC ≅ △ADE, and they correspond in order, so A corresponds to A, B corresponds to D, C corresponds to E, therefore the corresponding angles ∠CAB = ∠EAD. Let these two angles both be x, then x + 10° + x = 120°, so 2x = 110°, x = 55°. Therefore ∠CAB = 55°, ∠EAD = 55°. Since F is on AD, the included angle from AB to AD is ∠BAD = ∠BAC + ∠CAD = 55° + 10° = 65°. Also because ∠B = 30°, that is, the included angle between BC and BA is 30°; combined with B, C, F being collinear in the figure, ray FC is inclined downward by 30° compared with the horizontally rightward direction of AB. And ray FD is along the direction of AD, turned upward by 65° compared with the direction of AB. So ∠CFD = 30° + 65° = 95°.
